answer.reason: The AI system is deployed by a water utility to assist in managing critical digital infrastructure (water supply). Article 6(2) with Annex III, point 2 classifies as high-risk any AI system intended to be used as a safety component in the management and operation of critical digital infrastructure including the supply of water. The chatbot's role in handling customer enquiries about meter readings and payment plans, combined with the utility's management of water supply operations, brings it within this category.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It does not fall under Art. 5 prohibited practices. It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of products in Annex I) or Art. 6(2) (not listed in Annex III). However, it generates synthetic image content and is placed on the market, triggering Art. 50(2) transparency obligations to mark outputs as artificially generated in machine-readable format. This classification as limited_risk applies from 2 August 2026 when Art. 50 applies, and the company must comply by 2 December 2026 per Art. 111(4).

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It does not fall under Art. 5 prohibitions. It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of a product in Annex I) or Art. 6(2) (not listed in Annex III). However, it is designed to interact directly with natural persons and generates content (itineraries, recommendations), triggering Art. 50(1) transparency obligations to inform users they are interacting with an AI system. As a deployer placing the system into service in the Union, the company must comply with these transparency requirements.

The system is an AI-based text-to-speech synthesis system for audiobook generation, which falls within the scope of the EU AI Act as an AI system under Art. 3(1). It is not prohibited under Art. 5. It does not qualify as high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of products in Annex I) or Art. 6(2) (not listed in Annex III). However, Art. 50(2) applies: the system generates synthetic audio content, and the provider must ensure outputs are marked in machine-readable format as artificially generated. This transparency obligation places the system in the limited_risk category.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)). It does not fall under Art. 5 prohibitions. Article 50(2) applies: the company deploys an AI system generating synthetic video content and must mark outputs as artificially generated in machine-readable format. This transparency obligation makes it limited_risk rather than minimal_risk.

The system generates synthetic video and audio content of identifiable natural persons without consent, triggering Article 50(4) transparency obligations for deployers of deepfakes. Article 50(4) exempts content that forms part of an evidently artistic, creative, or satirical work, and the channel jingle and comedic context establish this as satirical. The system does not fall under Article 5 prohibitions because the satirical exception applies, and it is not high-risk under Annex III. Transparency obligations under Article 50(4) apply, requiring disclosure that content is artificially generated or manipulated in a manner appropriate to the satirical work.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It does not fall under Art. 5 prohibited practices. It is not high-risk under Art. 6 because it generates synthetic video content for entertainment purposes without depicting real persons, and thus does not trigger Annex III categories. However, Art. 50(2) applies: the provider of the generative video service must mark outputs as artificially generated in machine-readable format, and the deployer (the dairy) must ensure compliance with transparency obligations when the content is published to the public.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It does not fall under Art. 5 prohibitions. It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of harmonised products) or Art. 6(2) with Annex III (not listed there; administrative news generation does not match the enumerated use cases). Article 50(4) applies: the deployer generates and publishes text content with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest without human editorial review, triggering the transparency obligation to disclose that the text has been artificially generated or manipulated—unless the content has undergone human review or editorial control, which the description excludes ('ohne Gegenlesen'). This transparency duty places the system in limited_risk.

The newspaper deploys an AI writing tool to generate draft news content from notes and press releases, with mandatory human review and editorial approval before publication. This triggers Article 50(1) transparency obligations, as the AI system interacts with natural persons (readers) through generated content, requiring disclosure that content is AI-assisted. The system does not fall under prohibited practices (Art. 5), is not high-risk under Art. 6 (not a safety component, not listed in Annex III), and thus incurs transparency duties under Art. 50, classifying it as limited_risk.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)). It does not engage in prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) as it is not a safety component of products in Annex I, nor under Art. 6(2) and Annex III as document translation does not fall within any listed high-risk category and does not perform profiling. Art. 50 transparency obligations do not apply as the system does not interact directly with natural persons in the manner specified (users upload documents; no direct interaction like chatbots). The system therefore falls under minimal risk.

This is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)): a machine-based system that infers how to generate outputs (rewritten emails) from input. It does not fall under prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of a harmonised product) or Art. 6(2) and Annex III (not biometric, critical infrastructure, education, employment, essential services, law enforcement, migration, or justice-related). However, it triggers Art. 50(1) transparency obligations: it is an AI system intended to interact directly with natural persons (the email recipients see the rewritten output), so users must be informed they are interacting with an AI system unless this is obvious from context. This transparency duty places it in the limited_risk class.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)): a machine-based system that infers from voice input how to generate outputs controlling the coffee machine. It does not fall under Art. 5 prohibited practices, nor under Art. 6 high-risk criteria—it is neither a safety component of a product covered by Annex I nor listed in Annex III. The narrow procedural task exception (Art. 6(3)(a)) would apply even if Annex III applied. Art. 50 transparency obligations do not apply because the system does not interact directly with natural persons in a way requiring disclosure (the voice interaction is obvious). Therefore, minimal_risk applies.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)): it infers code suggestions from input. It does not engage in prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of products in Annex I) or Art. 6(2) (not listed in Annex III, as it performs a narrow procedural task of code completion without profiling or decision-making affecting fundamental rights). Art. 50 transparency obligations do not apply as the system does not interact directly with natural persons in the relevant sense—it assists developers in a professional tool context. Therefore, it is minimal_risk.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It does not fall under prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of products in Annex I) or Art. 6(2) (Annex III), as it performs a narrow procedural task of appointment rescheduling and does not materially influence outcomes affecting fundamental rights. However, Art. 50(1) applies: the AI system interacts directly with natural persons (patients) by telephone, and they must be informed that they are interacting with an AI system. This transparency obligation triggers limited_risk classification.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(b)). It does not fall under prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk: it is not a safety component of a product under Annex I (Art. 6(1)), and it does not fall under Annex III categories—it performs internal administrative assistance (answering IT and policy questions, drafting documents) without making decisions about employees or influencing critical outcomes. The Art. 6(3) exception applies: the system performs narrow procedural tasks and preparatory work, not decision-making. No transparency obligations under Art. 50 apply (no direct interaction with natural persons outside the organization, no synthetic content generation, no emotion recognition or biometric categorization). The system therefore carries only minimal risk.

The chatbot is an AI system intended to be used for recruitment and selection of natural persons, specifically to analyse and filter job applications and evaluate candidates, which falls under Annex III, point 4(a). The system makes decisions affecting access to employment by ranking applicants, and does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exceptions since it performs substantive evaluation rather than narrow procedural tasks or preparatory work, and materially influences the outcome of hiring decisions.

The payroll system is an AI system under Art. 3(1) as it infers outputs (pay calculations) from inputs (hours, rules) to influence decisions. It does not fall under Art. 5 prohibitions, Art. 6 high-risk criteria (not a safety component under Annex I, and does not match Annex III use cases—payroll calculation is not biometric identification, critical infrastructure management, education/vocational training, employment decisions, essential services eligibility, law enforcement, migration control, or judicial processes), nor Art. 50 transparency duties (it does not interact directly with natural persons or generate synthetic content). Therefore it is minimal_risk under Art. 2(1)(b) as a deployer located in the Union.

The system applies only explicit, rule-based filtering criteria (driver's license class, language level, location) without machine learning or trained models, and does not make autonomous decisions about candidates. While it is an AI system under Art. 3(1) as it processes inputs to generate filtered outputs, it does not fall under Art. 5 (prohibited practices), Art. 6 (high-risk), or Art. 50 (transparency obligations for interaction or synthetic content). The human reviewer retains full control and reviews filtered-out applications weekly.

The system is an AI system under Art. 3(1) as it infers ordering quantities from sales data to generate recommendations. It falls within the Act's scope under Art. 2(1)(b) as a deployer established in the Union. It does not engage prohibited practices under Art. 5, nor does it qualify as high-risk under Art. 6: it performs a narrow procedural task (averaging historical sales), is intended to improve a previously completed human activity (manual ordering), and does not materially influence decision-making as managers retain full override authority. Art. 50 transparency obligations do not apply as the system does not interact directly with natural persons or generate synthetic content. The system therefore incurs only minimal_risk obligations.

The system is an AI system within the scope of the Act (Art. 3(1)): it is a machine-based system that infers from input how to generate outputs (card selections) that can influence virtual environments. It is not prohibited (Art. 5), not high-risk (Art. 6), and does not trigger transparency obligations under Art. 50 because it does not interact directly with natural persons in a way that requires disclosure—the interaction is with game players who understand they are playing against a computer opponent. The system therefore falls under minimal_risk.

The system evaluates creditworthiness of natural persons to make credit decisions, falling under Annex III, point 5(b). Although the bank uses established logistic regression methodology, the system makes binding decisions on loan applications (automatic decline below threshold), materially influences the outcome of credit assessment, and does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exceptions as it is not a narrow procedural task, improvement of prior human activity, or preparatory task—it directly determines eligibility for essential financial services.

This AI system is excluded from the scope of the EU AI Act under Article 2(3), which states that the Regulation does not apply to AI systems placed on the market, put into service, or used exclusively for military, defence or national security purposes, regardless of the type of entity carrying out those activities. The software is designed solely for military reconnaissance and is supplied only to armed forces under defence procurement contracts.

The AI system is intended to be used for detecting and identifying natural persons in the context of border control and migration management (Annex III, point 7(d)), as evidenced by its original development for military troop movement tracking by the Bundeswehr. Although the company now markets it to forestry authorities, the same system is placed on the market under the provider's name for use by public authorities in migration, asylum and border control contexts, making it a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 7(d).

This AI system is developed and used exclusively for scientific research and development within a university group, with no placement on the market or putting into service. Article 2(6) of the EU AI Act explicitly excludes AI systems 'specifically developed and put into service for the sole purpose of scientific research and development.' The system is not placed on the market, not offered as a service, and access is restricted to the research group's own use.

The system is currently in research, testing and development phase prior to being placed on the market or put into service. Article 2(8) of the AI Act explicitly excludes research, testing or development activities regarding AI systems prior to their being placed on the market or put into service from the Regulation's scope. Since the prototype has never been deployed with real calls, has no pilot customer, and has not been placed on the market or put into service, it falls outside the scope of the AI Act.

The system is released under a free and open-source licence (Apache 2.0) and is not placed on the market or put into service as a high-risk AI system or under Article 5 or 50. Article 2(12) of the AI Act explicitly excludes AI systems released under free and open-source licences unless they are placed on the market or put into service as high-risk systems or fall under Article 5 or 50. This plant disease detection system does not fall under any prohibited practice in Article 5, is not high-risk under Article 6, and does not trigger the transparency obligations of Article 50 (it does not interact directly with natural persons in a way that requires disclosure, nor does it generate synthetic content). Therefore, the system is out of scope.

The system is an AI system intended to filter and rank job applications for recruitment decisions, falling under Annex III, point 4(a). Although based on open-source code, Article 2(12) exempts open-source AI systems only if they are not placed on the market or put into service as high-risk systems or systems under Articles 5 or 50; this system is placed into service as high-risk. The deployer's planned implementation—automatically rejecting all but the top 20 candidates—constitutes a high-risk recruitment system under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 4(a), as it materially influences hiring outcomes without the exception conditions in Article 6(3) applying.

The AI system is not placed on the market or put into service in the Union, and its output is not used in the Union. Article 2(1) requires the Regulation to apply to providers placing systems on the market in the Union or deployers located in the Union, or where output is used in the Union. This system operates exclusively in Texas with no Union presence or use.

The system is an AI-based portfolio management app used by a natural person for personal, non-professional investment purposes. Article 2(10) of the EU AI Act explicitly excludes AI systems used by natural persons in the course of purely personal non-professional activity from the Regulation's scope. The user is a teacher using the app solely for private retirement savings, not in any professional capacity or to advise others.

Article 5(1)(ba) prohibits placing on the market or putting into service an AI system that generates or manipulates realistic images of an identifiable natural person's intimate parts without freely-given, specific, informed, unambiguous and explicit consent. The app's core feature generates nude images of any person without consent, meeting this prohibition. Article 5(1a)(a) confirms the prohibition applies where generation of such material is the intended purpose of the AI system, which is clearly the case here.

The system generates synthetic intimate images of identifiable persons without their consent, which falls under Article 5(1)(ba) of the EU AI Act. This prohibition applies from 2 December 2026 according to Article 113(a), and the system was placed on the market on 1 September 2026, before the prohibition's entry into force. However, as of the assessment date (16 November 2026), the prohibition is imminent and the system clearly violates the requirements of Article 5(1)(ba) regarding non-consensual intimate image generation.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2). It does not fall under Art. 5 prohibited practices. It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of products in Annex I) or Art. 6(2) (not listed in Annex III). However, it generates synthetic image content and thus triggers Art. 50(2) transparency obligations requiring machine-readable marking of artificially generated outputs, which applies from 2 December 2026.

Article 5(1)(ba) prohibits placing on the market or putting into service AI systems that generate or manipulate realistic images of identifiable natural persons' intimate parts or engaged in sexually explicit activities without freely-given, specific, informed, unambiguous and explicit consent. Although the company obtained written consent from performers, Article 5(1a)(b) clarifies that use is prohibited where the deployer uses the system for generating such material. The company is deploying the software to generate sexually explicit deepfake content, which falls squarely within this prohibition applicable since 2 December 2026.

Article 5(1)(ba) prohibits placing into service or using an AI system that generates or manipulates realistic intimate images of identifiable natural persons without their freely-given, specific, informed, unambiguous and explicit consent. The company is deploying the commercial image generator to generate fake nude photos of named actresses and singers without consent and publishing them for profit. This constitutes a prohibited AI practice under Article 5(1)(ba), which has applied since 2 December 2026 (Article 113(3)(a)).

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)). It does not fall under Art. 5 prohibitions: it does not generate or manipulate intimate images (Art. 5(1)(ba)), but only blurs existing ones without creating new content, and Art. 5(1a)(a) requires generation or manipulation as the intended purpose or a reasonably foreseeable outcome—blurring is neither. It is not high-risk under Art. 6: it performs a narrow procedural task (image filtering) that does not materially influence decisions about persons (Art. 6(3)(a)). It triggers Art. 50 transparency obligations as a system interacting with users and processing image content, requiring disclosure of the blurring function.

The system generates child sexual abuse material (CSAM) as a reasonably foreseeable and reproducible outcome without adequate safeguards, violating Article 5(1)(bb) which prohibits placing on the market AI systems that generate material within the scope of Directive 2011/93/EU. Article 5(1a)(a)(ii) applies: the system's design, training, and capabilities make CSAM generation a foreseeable outcome without significant modification, and the provider has not implemented reasonable technical safety measures to prevent it. The prohibition applies from 2 December 2026 under Article 113(3)(a).

The system evaluates employee emotions (stress, irritation) during work and uses the results to make decisions affecting employment relationships, including performance evaluation and bonus calculation. This falls under Annex III, point 4(b), which covers AI systems for making decisions affecting work-related relationships and monitoring employee behavior. Article 6(3) exceptions do not apply as the system directly influences employment decisions rather than merely assisting human assessment.

The system performs biometric categorisation by inferring stress or panic states from biometric data (camera and wristband), which falls under Annex III, point 1(b). Although the deployer argues the system does not materially influence decision-making because it only triggers automated crane slowdown and supervisor alerts, Article 6(3) does not apply because the system performs profiling of natural persons (detecting acute psychological states), which the profiling carve-out in Article 6(3) explicitly excludes from exemption. The system is therefore high-risk.

The municipality deploys an AI system that evaluates eligibility of natural persons for essential public services (kindergarten places and sports facility access) based on a social scoring mechanism combining multiple behavioral data sources. This falls under Annex III, point 5(a), as it uses AI to determine access to essential public services. The system's use of behavioral monitoring (waste sorting, fines, engagement) to influence access to services constitutes a high-risk application under Article 6(2) and Annex III.

This AI system is deployed by a law enforcement authority to assess the risk of natural persons offending (committing burglary) based on profiling using personal characteristics, family background, neighbourhood, employment history and personality traits. It falls under Annex III, point 6(d), which covers AI systems assessing the risk of a natural person offending or re-offending not solely on the basis of profiling. The system does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exception because it materially influences the outcome of decision-making (determining who receives home visits and increased police stops) and performs profiling of natural persons, which triggers the mandatory high-risk classification under Article 6(3), final sentence.

The system creates facial recognition databases through untargeted scraping of facial images from the internet without consent, which is explicitly prohibited under Article 5(1)(e) of the EU AI Act. The system has been placed on the market since 2025 and continues to operate, making it a clear violation of the prohibition that applies from 2 February 2025.

The system categorizes individuals based on inferred sexual orientation and religious beliefs through facial analysis, which constitutes biometric categorization based on sensitive attributes prohibited under Article 5(1)(g) of the EU AI Act. This prohibition applies regardless of whether images are retained, as the inference and categorization itself violates the fundamental rights protection mandated by the regulation.

The AI system deploys manipulative techniques targeting children's vulnerabilities (age, emotional attachment to virtual pet) to materially distort their behaviour and cause them to make purchases they would not otherwise make, in violation of Article 5(1)(b). The system exploits the specific social and economic situation of minors and their cognitive development to induce spending decisions that cause significant financial harm to families.

The AI system deploys manipulative techniques with the objective of materially distorting the behaviour of natural persons by using artificial urgency ('only today', 'last warning before court') and personalised timing based on prior responses, causing them to take payment decisions they would not otherwise take. This violates Article 5(1)(a) of the EU AI Act, which prohibits AI systems that deploy purposefully manipulative or deceptive techniques with the objective or effect of materially distorting behaviour and causing significant harm.

Article 5(1)(h) prohibits real-time remote biometric identification in publicly accessible spaces for law enforcement unless strictly necessary for one of three objectives. The system's use for finding missing persons falls within Article 5(1)(h)(i), which is a permitted exception. However, the system will be deployed from 2028, after Article 5(1)(h) applies from 2 August 2026. The deployer has satisfied the procedural safeguards of Article 5(2)-(3) (prior judicial authorization, fundamental rights impact assessment, registration, notification). Since the use case and safeguards align with the statutory exception in Article 5(1)(h)(i), the system is not prohibited.

The supermarket chain deploys a remote biometric identification system at store entrances to match faces against a self-maintained database of persons banned for shoplifting. This falls under Annex III, point 1(a) as a remote biometric identification system. Article 6(3) does not apply because the system performs profiling of natural persons (matching against a maintained list) and thus remains high-risk regardless of the narrow procedural task exception.

The system is an AI system intended to be used for recruitment and selection of natural persons by analyzing and filtering job applications, falling under Annex III, point 4(a). By placing their name and trademark on the system without modifying it and reselling it to corporate clients, the company qualifies as a distributor under Article 3(7) and becomes a provider under Article 25(1)(a), subject to high-risk AI system obligations that apply from 2 December 2027 under Article 113(3)(c)(i).

The company uses an AI system to evaluate creditworthiness of natural persons and establish credit scores for consumer lending decisions, which falls under Annex III, point 5(b). Although the company is a deployer rather than the original provider, it has made substantial modifications to the system by retraining it with proprietary data and adding new input features (mobile payment histories), which under Article 25(1)(b) makes it a provider of the modified high-risk system. The system is placed on the market as of July 2026, before the application date of Chapter III requirements (2 December 2027 for Annex III systems per Article 113(3)(c)(i)), but the company must comply with high-risk requirements by that date.

The company deploys a general-purpose AI assistant to make recruitment decisions by filtering job applications and determining which candidates are invited or rejected. This falls squarely within Annex III, point 4(a), which covers AI systems intended to analyse and filter job applications and evaluate candidates. Article 6(3) does not apply because the system directly influences the outcome of hiring decisions without human review of rejected candidates, and the vendor's usage policy prohibition does not override the legal classification.

The system makes decisions affecting work-related relationships by automatically assigning tasks based on individual behaviour and performance metrics (pick rate, error rate), and by flagging underperforming workers for management review. This falls under Annex III, point 4(b), which covers AI systems intended to allocate tasks based on individual behaviour or personal traits or to monitor and evaluate performance in work relationships. The deployer is using the system under its authority in the Union and is therefore subject to high-risk AI system obligations under Article 6(2) and Chapter III.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(d)) that generates synthetic text content. It does not fall under prohibited practices (Art. 5) or high-risk categories (Art. 6, Annex I, Annex III). However, as a provider of an AI system generating synthetic text published to the public, it triggers transparency obligations under Art. 50(4) requiring disclosure that text has been artificially generated or manipulated when published with the purpose of informing the public on matters of public interest. The company acts as a distributor (Art. 3(7)) reselling under its own name without modification.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)): it infers outputs (answers) from inputs (customer questions) and can influence virtual environments (customer interactions). It does not fall under prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of products in Annex I) or Art. 6(2) (Annex III): it performs a narrow procedural task of customer service information provision without decision-making authority over customers, and thus qualifies for the Art. 6(3) exception. However, it is an AI system intended to interact directly with natural persons, triggering Art. 50(1) transparency obligations: users must be informed they are interacting with an AI system.

The firm is a deployer of a general-purpose AI assistant used for drafting, summarisation and translation tasks. These are narrow procedural tasks that do not fall under the high-risk categories in Annex III, and the system does not interact directly with natural persons or generate synthetic content for publication. Article 50 transparency obligations do not apply because the outputs are reviewed by a partner before any client-facing use and nothing is published by the AI system itself.

The essay-marking software is an AI system intended to evaluate learning outcomes of students in educational institutions, falling under Annex III, point 3(b). As an Austrian company placing on the market an AI system bearing the name and trademark of a Californian provider not established in the Union, you are an importer under Art. 3(6). The system materially influences the outcome of grading decisions and does not qualify for the Art. 6(3) exceptions, as it is not a narrow procedural task, does not merely improve a prior human activity, and performs substantive assessment rather than preparatory work.

The company is a distributor of recruitment AI software that evaluates job applications and ranks candidates, which falls under Annex III, point 4(a) (AI systems for recruitment and selection of natural persons). As a distributor making the system available on the Union market without modifying it, the company is subject to high-risk AI system obligations under Article 6(2) and Article 3(7). The system does not qualify for the Article 6(3) derogation since it directly influences hiring decisions rather than performing a narrow procedural task or preparatory function.

The company is a distributor placing an AI system on the market under its own name and trademark (Art. 3(7), Art. 25(1)(a)). The system evaluates creditworthiness and establishes risk pricing for natural persons in relation to life and health insurance, falling under Annex III, point 5(c). As a distributor making a substantial modification by rebranding and integrating the system into its own offering, the company becomes a provider subject to high-risk obligations under Article 16.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(d)). It does not engage in prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk: it does not fall under Art. 6(1) (not a safety component of a regulated product) or Art. 6(2) (Annex III). The system performs a narrow procedural task (inventory forecasting) with human review of suggestions, and does not profile natural persons or materially influence consequential decisions about them. It therefore falls outside Art. 6(3) high-risk criteria. No transparency obligations under Art. 50 apply, as the system does not interact directly with natural persons or generate synthetic content. The importer is subject only to minimal-risk obligations.

The system evaluates creditworthiness of natural persons to establish credit scores for lending decisions, falling under Annex III, point 5(b). Although the vendor remains the nominal provider, the deployer has made substantial modifications by adding behavioural inputs (app session data, hesitation patterns) that materially alter the system's decision-making basis, triggering deployer obligations under Article 25(1)(b) as a provider of the modified high-risk system.

The system is used to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits (housing allowance/Wohngeld) and to make preliminary decisions on granting or refusing such benefits, falling under Annex III, point 5(a). Although human signature remains, the AI system materially influences the outcome of decision-making by pre-classifying applications, and the deployer's modification of the original software to this purpose makes it a high-risk system under Article 6(2) and (3).

DermaSight is an AI system intended to be used to evaluate eligibility for essential public services (healthcare referral decisions) and assist in clinical decision-making affecting access to medical services. It falls under Annex III, point 5(a), as an AI system intended to be used by public authorities or on their behalf to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits and services, including healthcare services. Although the GP retains final decision-making authority, the system's output materially influences the outcome of the clinical assessment and referral decision, triggering high-risk classification under Article 6(2) and (3)—the narrow procedural task and human review exceptions do not apply because the system performs substantive medical assessment rather than a preparatory task.

The AI system is a predictive maintenance tool that analyzes operational data (trips, door cycles, motor currents) to forecast wear part replacement and optimize technician scheduling and spare parts ordering. It does not control lift safety systems or steering mechanisms, only reads data. Under Article 6(3), an AI system referred to in Annex III is not high-risk where it performs a narrow procedural task, improves results of previously completed human activity, or performs a preparatory task. This system qualifies as a narrow procedural task (maintenance scheduling) and preparatory task (planning), with human technicians retaining full control. It therefore falls outside high-risk classification and, having no transparency obligations under Article 50, is subject only to minimal_risk requirements.

Pip is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)): a machine-based system that infers from input how to generate outputs (conversation) that can influence physical or virtual environments. It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It does not meet high-risk criteria under Art. 6(1) because although it is a toy covered by Annex I (Directive 2009/48/EC), it is not required to undergo third-party conformity assessment—the provider performed self-assessment under harmonised standards without a notified body (Art. 6(1)(b) not fulfilled). It is not listed in Annex III. However, as an AI system intended to interact directly with natural persons (children), it falls under Art. 50(1) transparency obligations, making it limited_risk.

The AI system is a safety component of a loader crane (a machine covered by Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 in Annex I, Section A, point 21) that prevents tip-over and overload by controlling crane movements. The product requires third-party conformity assessment by a notified body under the Machinery Regulation. Article 6(1) therefore classifies this as high-risk.

The automatic emergency braking system is an AI system (Art. 3(1)) that qualifies as a safety component of motor vehicles covered by Regulation (EU) 2018/858 and (EU) 2019/2144 listed in Annex I, Section A. It undergoes third-party conformity assessment as part of EU vehicle type-approval before placing on the market (Art. 6(1)). Therefore it is high-risk under Annex I, point 11 (motor vehicles and their safety components).

The smart speaker 'Kiez' is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It does not fall under prohibited practices (Art. 5). It is not high-risk under Art. 6(1) because it is not a safety component of a product covered by Annex I Section A, and the third-party conformity assessment concerns only radio spectrum use, not health and safety (Art. 6(1)(c)). It does not fall under Annex III high-risk categories. However, the system generates synthetic audio content (Art. 50(2)), triggering transparency obligations to mark outputs as artificially generated in machine-readable format, which classifies it as limited_risk.

The system is a safety component of grinding machines covered by Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 on machinery (Annex I, Section A, point 21), and the machines require third-party conformity assessment under that legislation. Article 6(1) classifies such AI systems as high-risk. However, confirmation is needed on whether the system qualifies as a safety component under Article 6(1a)-(1b) (the description suggests it does, as failure would endanger health and safety), and whether the machinery directive's conformity assessment requirement applies to the retrofit kit specifically or only to the integrated machine.

The system does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exception because it performs profiling of natural persons by inferring personality traits and emotional states from their biometric data, which the regulation explicitly excludes from derogation.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It qualifies as high-risk under Annex III, point 2, as it is intended to be used as a safety component in the management and operation of critical infrastructure (water supply), where failure or malfunction would endanger health and safety by controlling chlorine dosing and shutting down the outlet to prevent unsafe water reaching consumers (Art. 6(2), 6(1b)). The Art. 6(3) derogation does not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of safety-critical decision-making and is not merely a narrow procedural task or preparatory step.

The system is an AI system intended to be used as a safety component in the management and operation of critical infrastructure (road traffic), as it autonomously controls dynamic speed limits and lane closures on motorways based on real-time data. This falls under Annex III, point 2. The deployer is a regional traffic control center operating the system under its own authority in the Union.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It falls under Annex III, point 3(a) as an AI system intended to determine access or admission to educational institutions. The deployer has not documented that it qualifies for the Art. 6(3) exception, and the system materially influences admission outcomes without proper human review of most decisions, so it remains high-risk.

CodeMark is an AI system intended to evaluate learning outcomes of students in educational institutions by assigning marks that directly affect course grades, falling under Annex III, point 3(b). The system is used by universities to determine student assessment outcomes, which materially influences educational decisions. As the provider placing this system on the market, the company must comply with high-risk AI system requirements under Article 6(2) and Chapter III.

The AI system evaluates learning outcomes and steers the learning process by determining which modules are unlocked and which exercises students receive based on competency assessment. This falls under Annex III, point 3(b) (AI systems for evaluating learning outcomes to steer the learning process in educational institutions). The school is a deployer using the system under its authority in an educational context.

The system is used to determine access or admission to educational institutions (secondary schools) based on AI assessment of student performance data. This falls under Annex III, point 3(a), which classifies AI systems intended to determine access or admission to educational institutions as high-risk. The bus route planning module is a separate non-high-risk system and does not affect this classification.

The system is an AI system intended to determine access to educational institutions by assigning natural persons to educational levels (A1-C1), which falls under Annex III, point 3(a). Although the school can override the placement, the system materially influences the outcome of the decision-making process regarding course access, and does not qualify for the Article 6(3) derogation because it performs a substantive assessment rather than a narrow procedural task, preparatory task, or mere improvement of prior human activity.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It falls under Annex III, point 3(d) as an AI system intended to monitor and detect prohibited behaviour of students during tests in educational institutions. The university is a deployer using the system under its authority (Art. 3(4)). The Art. 6(3) exception does not apply: the system materially influences the outcome of decision-making (exam voidance) and performs profiling of natural persons by detecting their location and device use, triggering the profiling rule in Art. 6(3).

The company deploys an AI system intended to filter and rank job applications for recruitment purposes, which falls under Annex III, point 4(a) (AI systems for recruitment and selection of natural persons, including filtering job applications). The automatic rejection threshold at 40 points does not qualify as a narrow procedural task, improvement of prior human activity, or preparatory task under Article 6(3), as it materially influences the outcome of recruitment decisions. This is a high-risk AI system requiring compliance with Chapter III requirements applicable from 2 December 2027.

JobReach is an AI system intended to be used for recruitment and selection of natural persons by analyzing and filtering job applications and placing targeted job advertisements based on inferred characteristics. This falls squarely within Annex III, point 4(a). The system makes decisions about which users see job adverts based on their inferred skills, location, and likelihood to apply, which constitutes filtering and targeting for recruitment purposes. Article 6(3) exceptions do not apply: the system is not performing a narrow procedural task, is not merely improving a prior human activity, and directly influences the outcome of recruitment decisions by determining audience exposure.

The system is used to make decisions affecting work-related relationships and termination of employment contracts based on individual behaviour and performance characteristics, falling squarely under Annex III, point 4(b). Article 6(3) does not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of termination decisions and performs profiling of natural persons, which triggers the mandatory high-risk classification under Article 6(3), final sentence.

The system evaluates and classifies employee performance based on behavioral monitoring (conversation duration, pauses, keyboard and mouse activity, customer ratings) and materially influences decisions on contract renewal. This falls under Annex III, point 4(b), which covers AI systems intended to make decisions affecting work-related relationships and termination of contractual relationships based on individual behavior or personal traits. The system does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exception because it directly influences employment decisions rather than merely assisting human review.

The system is deployed by a public authority to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits (disability allowance) and to grant, reduce, or revoke such benefits. This falls squarely within Annex III, point 5(a). Although human assessors formally sign decisions, the system's recommendations are rarely departed from, indicating material influence over the outcome. The system does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exception because it performs profiling of natural persons and materially influences decision-making on essential benefits.

The AI system is intended to be used by public authorities to evaluate eligibility for essential public assistance benefits (housing allowance) and to grant, reduce, revoke or reclaim such benefits, falling under Annex III, point 5(a). The company is the provider as it developed the system, placed it on the market under its own name, and operates it in its own data center for the municipalities.

The system evaluates creditworthiness of natural persons to establish credit decisions (pay-later approval and limits), which falls under Annex III, point 5(b). The creditworthiness assessment for granting or denying credit is a high-risk use case under the AI Act, as it directly influences access to essential financial services and can cause significant harm to individuals through unfair denial of credit.

The AI system evaluates creditworthiness of natural persons to make credit decisions, falling under Annex III, point 5(b). Although the system does not solely determine the outcome (human review occurs above a threshold), it materially influences the decision-making process by automatically rejecting applications below the threshold, and thus does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exception for narrow procedural tasks or preparatory assessments. The Sparkasse is a deployer using the system under its authority.

The AI system evaluates creditworthiness and establishes credit scores by assessing expected claims to set insurance premiums and determine coverage exclusions for natural persons. This falls under Annex III, point 5(c), which covers AI systems for risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons in life and health insurance. The system is placed on the market under the company's own brand and is therefore a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) and Annex III.

The system evaluates creditworthiness and risk assessment for life and health insurance pricing decisions affecting natural persons, falling under Annex III, point 5(c). As the insurance company using the AI system under its authority to make underwriting decisions, the company is a deployer subject to high-risk AI system obligations under Article 6(2) and Annex III.

The AI system evaluates and classifies emergency calls and establishes priority in dispatching emergency first response services (ambulances), falling under Annex III, point 5(d). As the operator deploying this system in the Union to triage emergency healthcare calls and dispatch decisions, the company is a deployer subject to high-risk AI system obligations under Article 6(2) and Article 3(4).

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It qualifies as high-risk under Annex III, point 5(d), as it is intended to evaluate and classify emergency calls and establish priority in dispatching emergency first response services, including emergency healthcare patient triage systems. The system's role in determining patient queue priority in emergency departments directly matches this provision.

The system is a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 6(a), as it is intended to be used by law enforcement authorities to assess the risk of natural persons becoming victims of criminal offences (scams targeting older people). The system infers vulnerability based on age, living situation, and prior reports, making it a risk assessment tool for victimisation. Article 6(3) does not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of decision-making (determining which residents receive prevention visits) and performs profiling of natural persons based on age and social characteristics.

The system assesses the risk of natural persons offending or re-offending based on past criminal behaviour and is used by law enforcement authorities (the federal police) to support law enforcement decision-making. Article 6(2) with Annex III, point 6(d) classifies such AI systems as high-risk. Although the system is limited to objective facts and human review occurs, it still falls within the high-risk category as a risk assessment tool for criminal offending used by law enforcement.

The system is deployed by a law enforcement authority (Landeskriminalamt) to assess the risk of natural persons offending or re-offending and to profile natural persons in the course of criminal investigation. Article 6(2) read with Annex III, point 6(d) classifies such AI systems as high-risk. The system's core function—creating profiles with contact networks, movement patterns, and group roles, then recommending primary suspects—constitutes profiling for criminal investigation purposes, triggering high-risk classification under Annex III, point 6(d).

The system is an AI system within the Act's scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(a)). It is not prohibited under Art. 5. It falls under Annex III, point 7(b), as it assesses risk posed by natural persons entering EU territory in the migration and border control context. The system does not qualify for the Art. 6(3) derogation because it performs profiling of natural persons (Art. 6(3), final sentence), making it always high-risk regardless of narrow task or preparatory function.

The port health authority uses an AI system to assess health risks of ship passengers and crew to determine who undergoes medical examination before disembarkation. This falls under Annex III, point 5(a), as an AI system intended to be used by a public authority to evaluate eligibility for essential public health services. The system materially influences the outcome of the health screening decision and does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exceptions, as it performs a core assessment function rather than a narrow procedural task or preparatory activity.

The AI system is used by a public authority (immigration office) to assist in examining applications for residence permits and assessing eligibility of natural persons applying for a status, which falls under Annex III, point 7(c). The system processes personal data and makes recommendations that materially influence the outcome of administrative decisions on work-related residence permits, making it a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) and Annex III.

The system is an AI system within scope (Art. 3(1), 2(1)(b)). It is not prohibited (Art. 5). It falls under Annex III, point 7(d) as an AI system intended to be used by competent public authorities in the context of border control management for the purpose of detecting natural persons. The Art. 6(3) exception does not apply because the system performs detection of natural persons, which materially influences the outcome of border control decisions and is not merely a narrow procedural task, preparatory task, or improvement of prior human activity. As a deployer placing the system into service, you are subject to high-risk obligations under Art. 16 from 2 December 2027 (Art. 113(3)(c)(i)).

The system deploys real-time remote biometric identification (facial recognition) in a publicly accessible space (reception facility) for purposes of identifying and monitoring persons. This falls under Annex III, point 1(a) (remote biometric identification systems). Article 5(1)(h) permits such use only for law enforcement purposes meeting strict conditions; the migration authority's use for general facility management and security does not qualify as law enforcement under those provisions. The system is therefore high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III, point 1(a).

This AI system is intended to assist judicial authorities in applying the law to concrete facts in asylum and tax cases, falling squarely within Annex III, point 8(a). The system materially influences the outcome of judicial decision-making by generating proposed judgments that judges then edit and sign, and does not qualify for the Article 6(3) exceptions since it performs core judicial reasoning rather than a narrow procedural task, preparatory work, or mere improvement of completed human activity. As a deployer of this high-risk AI system, the court is subject to the obligations in Chapter III, which apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems.

The AI system is intended to assist judicial authorities (here: recognized consumer dispute resolution bodies) in researching and interpreting facts and law and in applying the law to concrete facts by generating dispute resolution proposals. This falls squarely under Annex III, point 8(a), which covers AI systems assisting in the administration of justice. The system's role in influencing the outcome of alternative dispute resolution proceedings makes it high-risk under Article 6(2) and Annex III.

The system is designed to influence voting behaviour by segmenting voters, predicting persuasive arguments, and generating tailored ads shown to undecided voters before elections with the explicit aim of shifting their vote. This falls squarely under Annex III, point 8(b), which covers AI systems intended to influence the outcome of elections or the voting behaviour of natural persons. The system's output (tailored political ads) is directly exposed to natural persons, so the carve-out for tools used only for administrative or logistical purposes does not apply.

The system is an AI system within the Act's scope (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It is not prohibited under Art. 5. It falls under Annex III, point 3(a), as it is intended to determine access or admission to educational institutions. The Art. 6(3) exception does not apply because the system materially influences the outcome of decision-making by ranking applicants for admission; it is not a narrow procedural task, does not merely improve a prior human activity, and performs profiling of natural persons through the proctoring and scoring model.

The HR suite performs recruitment filtering and candidate evaluation for job applications (Annex III, point 4(a)), and creates performance rankings that materially influence promotion decisions affecting work-related relationships (Annex III, point 4(b)). Both uses fall under high-risk AI systems for employment and workers' management. The deployer must comply with Chapter III requirements applicable from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems.

The mortgage scoring model is a high-risk AI system under Annex III, point 5(b), as it evaluates creditworthiness of natural persons to establish credit scoring for lending decisions. The insurance pricing module is also high-risk under Annex III, point 5(c), as it performs risk assessment and pricing in relation to natural persons for life and health insurance. As deployers using these systems under your authority, you are subject to the obligations in Chapter III of the AI Act, which applies from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems.

The AI system is a safety component of a Class IIb medical device (insulin pump) covered by Regulation (EU) 2017/745 listed in Annex I, Section A, point 11. The medical device is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment by a notified body. Article 6(1) therefore classifies this as high-risk AI.

The system is an AI-based in vitro diagnostic medical device (class C) that is a safety component of a product covered by Annex I, Section A (Regulation (EU) 2017/746 on in vitro diagnostic medical devices), and it undergoes third-party conformity assessment by a notified body. Under Article 6(1), it qualifies as high-risk. The company is a provider under Article 3(3), placing the system on the market in the Union.

The neural network is a safety component of a lift product covered by Directive 2014/33/EU (listed in Annex I, Section A). The lift is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment under that Directive. Article 6(1) therefore classifies this AI system as high-risk. The system's failure would endanger health and safety, meeting Article 6(1b).

The airbag vest is a personal protective equipment (PPE) Category III product covered by Regulation (EU) 2016/425 listed in Annex I, Section A. The neural network AI system functions as a safety component by detecting falls and triggering the airbag deployment, which is essential to the product's safety function. Since the product requires third-party conformity assessment (notified body testing), the AI system meets both conditions of Article 6(1) and is therefore high-risk.

The neural network control unit is a safety component of tower cranes, which are machinery products covered by Regulation (EU) 2023/1230 (Annex I, Section A, point 21). The system prevents tipping and load swing hazards, making it a safety-critical component that undergoes third-party conformity assessment by a notified body. Article 6(1) classifies such AI systems as high-risk.

The emergency braking system is a safety component of motor vehicles covered by Regulation (EU) 2019/2144 (listed in Annex I, Section A, point 19), and the vehicle manufacturer is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment for market placement. As the developer and supplier placing the system on the market under its own name, the company qualifies as a provider of a high-risk AI system under Article 6(1).

The trackside detector is an AI system (Art. 3(1)) that is a safety component of railway infrastructure covered by Directive (EU) 2016/797 (Annex I, Section A, point 17). The system is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment by a notified body against EU railway interoperability requirements before placing on the market (Art. 6(1)). Both conditions for high-risk classification under Art. 6(1) are fulfilled.

The AI system is a safety component of an agricultural vehicle (tractor) covered by Regulation (EU) No 167/2013 listed in Annex I, Section A, point 15. The system is required to undergo third-party conformity assessment (EU type-approval) as a condition for placing the product on the market, fulfilling both conditions of Article 6(1). The obstacle and person detection function is safety-critical as its failure or malfunction would endanger health and safety under Article 6(1b).

The criminal police authority is deploying an AI system (digital polygraph) intended to be used by law enforcement authorities to assess the reliability of evidence in the course of investigation or prosecution of criminal offences. This falls under Annex III, point 6(b), which classifies such systems as high-risk. The system's output directly influences investigative decisions and suspect classification, making it a high-risk AI system under Article 6(2) and Annex III.

The system is an AI system within the scope of the EU AI Act (Art. 3(1), Art. 2(1)(a)). It is not prohibited under Art. 5. It falls under Annex III, point 6(c), as an AI system intended to be used by law enforcement authorities to evaluate the reliability of evidence in the course of investigation or prosecution of criminal offences. The system does not qualify for the Art. 6(3) exception because it performs profiling or materially influences the outcome of decision-making (likelihood ratios directly inform prosecutorial and judicial decisions on suspect involvement). As a provider placing the system on the market in the Union, the company is subject to high-risk requirements under Art. 16 and related provisions.
